newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Credit Lyonnais posts increased 1996 profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Credit Lyonnais posts increased 1996 profit.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais, the French bank which nearly collapsed under the weight of its lending excesses, on Thursday reported an increased profit for 1996 and a big improvement in underlying performance.

The state-controlled bank, which the centre-right government plans to recapitalise and privatise by early 1999, said net attributable profit rose to 202 million francs ($35.5 million) from a 1995 profit of 13 million francs.
The results of the bank, which has already received two large state bailouts, were in line with market expectations.
The figures included charges of 2.48 billion francs for restructuring and 200 million francs to prepare for the move to European monetary union in 1999.
They also included a 107 million franc payment to the state under terms of a 1995 state bailout which stipulated it had to earmark a portion of its profits for the public purse.

Net banking income was virtually flat at 44.5 billion francs compared with 43.4 billion in 1995 but rose 5.9 percent on a like-for-like base, helped by strong international activity and thriving capital markets.
Commissions jumped 7.9 percent and 13 percent on a like-for-like basis, boosted by contributions from financial services and the distribution of insurance products.
Gross operating profit rose 42 percent to 9.5 billion francs, reflecting better cost control and higher banking income, the bank said in a statement.
"This mastering of general costs comes form the group's restructuring efforts. Personnel costs were down 1.0 per cent on a like for like basis," it said.
All of the bank's four profit centres showed a rise in profits. In France, net pretax profits showed a sharp recovery, helped by lower costs and staff cuts.
Outside France, European operations posted a 34 percent rise in gross operating profit with provisions down 20 percent reflecting healthier loan portfolios.
Gross operating profits from commercial banking in the rest of the world soared 60 percent, reflecting good performances in North and South Ameria, Asia and elsewhere.

The bank, whose ill-fated expansion drive in the late 1980s and early 1990s briefly made it the biggest bank outside Japan, said its recovery plan involved mantaining a broad-based commercial banking network at home and focusing on merchant banking and financial markets abroad.

This will mean hiving off many of its foreign banking units across Europe to satisfy demands imposed by the European Commission in exchange for approval of the government's bailout plan, the fourth in three years, to be presented by early April.
Despite the bank's strong performance, it will still need a big dose of public money to prepare it for privatisation.
The bank is expected to need a 10 to 15 billion franc injection of public money to boost solvency ratios and cover losses on asset sales sought by the EU in exchange for sanctioning the aid.

The European Commission, which only two years ago approved a 45 billion franc bailout for the bank, has estimated another 15 to 20 billion francs in state money could be needed to soften the terms of a loan the bank made under the 1995 rescue to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.
But those sums pale beside estimates of the final cost of saving the bank. Latest figures suggest the total bill could top 130 billion francs. $ = 5.686 French Francs)
